title: 1 Chronicles 16:8–36
context: 1 Chronicles 16:8–36 is one psalm, presented as the thanksgiving David committed to Asaph and his brothers on the day the ark came to Jerusalem. It is kept here as a single unit of twenty-nine verses. Its lines closely parallel material in the Psalter: 16:8–22 parallels Psalm 105:1–15; 16:23–33 parallels Psalm 96; 16:34 matches the opening call of Psalm 106:1; and 16:35–36 parallels Psalm 106:47–48. The wording differs in places, and the differences are named rather than harmonized. Among the useful examples: “offspring of Israel” (16:13) where Psalm 105:6 has “you offspring of Abraham, his servant”; “Remember his covenant forever” (16:15) where Psalm 105:8 has “He has remembered his covenant forever”; and Chronicles’ psalm ends its Psalm 96 section with “for he comes to judge the earth” and does not include the closing lines of Psalm 96:13. Interpreters discuss how the Chronicles setting and the Psalter relate, and this draft takes no position. The psalm is largely shared ground about remembering the LORD’s covenant, praising him among the nations, and calling on him to save. Questions already treated in existing boxes at Psalm 105:6, Psalm 105:8, and Psalm 96:1 are not reopened here.

verses.text: Oh give thanks to the LORD. Call on his name. Make what he has done known among the peoples.
verses.arminianNotes:
The psalm opens with the call to give thanks to the LORD, call on his name, and make what he has done known among the peoples. The parallel is Psalm 105:1.

Arminian readers hear a call that reaches outward to the peoples, and they see God’s works made known so that others may hear and respond to the God of Israel.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers hear the same outward call and stress that the content of the proclamation is what God has done, so that praise rests on God’s acts rather than human achievement.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground: thanksgiving, prayer, and witness belong together, and the psalm’s opening sets the tone of remembrance for the whole song that follows.

verses.text: Sing to him. Sing praises to him. Tell of all his marvelous works.
verses.arminianNotes:
The people are called to sing to him, sing praises to him, and tell of all his marvelous works. The parallel is Psalm 105:2.

Arminian readers see joyful participation invited from all who hear, and they note that telling God’s works is a responsibility each worshiper is called to take up gladly in daily life and in the gathered assembly.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the marvelous works recounted in the psalm are the LORD’s deeds for his covenant people, and that praise in Scripture is often a retelling of what God has done in history.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about praise that tells the story of God’s faithfulness and treat it without contrast.

verses.text: Glory in his holy name. Let the heart of those who seek the LORD rejoice.
verses.arminianNotes:
The people are called to glory in his holy name, and the heart of those who seek the LORD is to rejoice. The parallel is Psalm 105:3.

Arminian readers note that seeking the LORD is presented as an activity of his people, and they see joy promised to those who genuinely seek him, a fitting theme in a book that often speaks of seeking God.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the holy name is the ground of boasting, so that God’s people glory not in themselves but in the LORD, and they see the joy of seekers as the fruit of God’s presence among them.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about joy in seeking God, especially fitting after the lesson of chapter 13.

verses.text: Seek the LORD and his strength. Seek his face forever more.
verses.arminianNotes:
The people are called to seek the LORD and his strength and to seek his face forevermore. The parallel is Psalm 105:4.

Arminian readers see a lifelong calling to continue seeking God, and they note that the psalm’s repeated call to seek fits Chronicles’ concern that Israel seek the LORD rather than neglect him as in the days of Saul (13:3).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that God’s strength is sought because his people have none of their own to rely on, and they see the call to seek his face as an invitation to communion with the God who has drawn near.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground and do not divide over the call to seek God.

verses.text: Remember his marvelous works that he has done, his wonders, and the judgments of his mouth,
verses.arminianNotes:
The people are called to remember his marvelous works, his wonders, and the judgments of his mouth. The parallel is Psalm 105:5.

Arminian readers note that remembering is an act of faith that God’s people are called to practice, and they see memory of God’s past works as a safeguard against forgetting him in the present.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the judgments of his mouth refer to God’s spoken decisions and acts of justice on behalf of his people, and they see remembrance as rooted in God’s own self-revelation.

Both traditions read the phrase as shared ground and do not use it to raise a debate; the psalm calls for grateful memory of God’s word and works.

verses.text: you offspring of Israel his servant, you children of Jacob, his chosen ones.
verses.arminianNotes:
The psalm addresses “you offspring of Israel his servant, you children of Jacob, his chosen ones.” The parallel in Psalm 105:6 reads “you offspring of Abraham, his servant”, and the difference is noted rather than harmonized.

Arminian readers hear the covenant people addressed as a whole, called to remember and to praise.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise hear the address to Israel as God’s chosen people. The question of how this choosing relates to individual salvation is treated in the existing box at Psalm 105:6 and is not reopened here.

Both traditions read the verse in its setting as shared ground: Israel is called to remember the God who chose them as his people.

verses.text: He is the LORD our God. His judgments are in all the earth.
verses.arminianNotes:
The psalm declares, “He is the LORD our God. His judgments are in all the earth.” The parallel is Psalm 105:7.

Arminian readers note that the God of Israel’s covenant is also the judge of all the earth, and they see his universal rule as the ground for the psalm’s call to make his works known among the peoples.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note the same move from the particular to the universal and stress that the LORD who is Israel’s God rules over every nation, so that his judgments are not limited to one people.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about God’s covenant relationship with Israel and his rule over all the earth, without a contrast over his judgments.

verses.text: Remember his covenant forever, the word which he commanded to a thousand generations,
verses.arminianNotes:
The psalm calls, “Remember his covenant forever, the word which he commanded to a thousand generations” The parallel in Psalm 105:8 reads “He has remembered his covenant forever”. Chronicles calls the people to remember, while the Psalter speaks of God remembering.

Arminian readers see the people summoned to grateful covenant memory.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the people’s remembering rests on God’s own faithfulness to his word across generations. The questions about covenant remembrance treated in the existing box at Psalm 105:8 are not reopened here.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground and record the difference in wording between the two settings without harmonizing it.

verses.text: the covenant which he made with Abraham, his oath to Isaac.
verses.arminianNotes:
The covenant is the one God made with Abraham, his oath to Isaac. The parallel is Psalm 105:9.

Arminian readers note that the covenant is rooted in God’s personal dealings with the patriarchs, and they see the oath as a promise that invites trust and faithful response from each generation that hears it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that the covenant rests on God’s oath, which underlines that its security lies in God’s commitment rather than in human performance (compare Genesis 22:16–18).

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about the patriarchal covenant and the faithfulness of God that the psalm calls Israel to remember and celebrate.

verses.text: He confirmed it to Jacob for a statute, and to Israel for an everlasting covenant,
verses.arminianNotes:
God confirmed the covenant to Jacob for a statute and to Israel for an everlasting covenant. The parallel is Psalm 105:10.

Arminian readers note that the covenant passes from generation to generation, and they see each generation called to embrace it and live within it with faith and obedience, as Israel does at the ark’s arrival.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the covenant is called everlasting, and they see God’s commitment continuing from Abraham to Isaac to Jacob as evidence that his promises do not lapse with the passing of generations.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about the continuity of God’s covenant with Israel.

verses.text: saying, “I will give you the land of Canaan, The lot of your inheritance,”
verses.arminianNotes:
God’s promise is quoted: “I will give you the land of Canaan, The lot of your inheritance” The parallel in Psalm 105:11 reads “To you I will give the land of Canaan”.

Arminian readers see the gift of the land as God’s gracious promise to a people who did not yet possess it, and they note that the promise called for trust in God while the patriarchs were still wanderers.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the land as an inheritance assigned by God, not earned, and they note that the psalm recalls the promise at the moment the ark comes to rest in the land God gave.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about the land promise and record the small difference in wording.

verses.text: when you were but a few men in number, yes, very few, and foreigners in it.
verses.arminianNotes:
The psalm recalls the time “when you were but a few men in number, yes, very few, and foreigners in it.” The parallel in Psalm 105:12 reads “when they were but a few men in number”.

Arminian readers note that Chronicles’ second-person wording draws the worshipers directly into the story.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that God’s choice of a small and vulnerable family highlights grace, since the promise did not rest on the patriarchs’ strength or numbers (compare Deuteronomy 7:7).

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about God’s faithfulness to a few wandering foreigners, and they record the difference in person between the two settings without harmonizing it.

verses.text: They went about from nation to nation, from one kingdom to another people.
verses.arminianNotes:
The patriarchs went about from nation to nation, from one kingdom to another people. The parallel is Psalm 105:13.

Arminian readers see the patriarchs’ wandering as a life of faith lived without security in the land, and they note that God’s people are often called to trust him while their circumstances remain uncertain and unsettled.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the wandering of the patriarchs was under God’s watchful care at every stage, as the next verses make clear, so that their insecurity was held within his promise.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about a people sustained by God’s promise while they were still landless sojourners.

verses.text: He allowed no man to do them wrong. Yes, he reproved kings for their sakes,
verses.arminianNotes:
God allowed no man to do them wrong and reproved kings for their sakes. The parallel is Psalm 105:14.

Arminian readers note that God protected the patriarchs while they made real choices and sometimes failed, and they see his protection as faithful care for those he had called into covenant with himself.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see God’s sovereign protection of his people even over kings, and they connect the verse with episodes such as Genesis 12:17 and 20:3, where God warns rulers on behalf of the patriarchs.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about God guarding his people and his promise among the nations.

verses.text: “Don’t touch my anointed ones! Do my prophets no harm!”
verses.arminianNotes:
God’s word to the kings is quoted: “Don’t touch my anointed ones! Do my prophets no harm!” The parallel is Psalm 105:15.

Arminian readers note that in this psalm the anointed ones and prophets are the patriarchs, and they caution against reading the verse as a general shield placing leaders beyond accountability.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers agree that the context concerns the patriarchs whom God protected, and they see the verse as an expression of God’s care for those he had set apart for his purposes.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about God’s protection of his chosen servants, and both avoid using it to excuse leaders from correction.

verses.text: Sing to the LORD, all the earth! Display his salvation from day to day.
verses.arminianNotes:
The psalm turns to the whole earth: “Sing to the LORD, all the earth! Display his salvation from day to day.” This section parallels Psalm 96, beginning with lines that correspond to Psalm 96:1–2.

Arminian readers hear a call addressed to all the earth.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers hear the same universal summons and see the salvation of Israel’s God as news meant for every nation. The questions concerning the new song treated in the existing box at Psalm 96:1 are not reopened here, and Chronicles’ version does not include the phrase about a new song.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about worldwide praise.

verses.text: Declare his glory among the nations, and his marvelous works among all the peoples.
verses.arminianNotes:
The people are told to declare his glory among the nations and his marvelous works among all the peoples. The parallel is Psalm 96:3.

Arminian readers see a mission reaching beyond Israel, and they note that the glory of God is meant to be made known so that the nations may hear and turn to him in faith and worship.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the glory declared is God’s own, and they see Israel’s worship as a witness to the nations, a theme that the New Testament develops in the mission to the Gentiles.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about proclaiming God’s glory among the nations and treat it without contrast.

verses.text: For great is the LORD, and greatly to be praised. He also is to be feared above all gods.
verses.arminianNotes:
“For great is the LORD, and greatly to be praised. He also is to be feared above all gods.” The parallel is Psalm 96:4.

Arminian readers see the greatness of God as the reason for praise, and they note that the fear of the LORD is a reverent awe that draws worshipers near rather than driving them away from his presence.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the LORD’s greatness sets him above all rivals, and they see the call to fear him as especially fitting after the death of Uzza and the careful second procession.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about the greatness of God and the reverence due to him above every so-called god.

verses.text: For all the gods of the peoples are idols, but the LORD made the heavens.
verses.arminianNotes:
“For all the gods of the peoples are idols, but the LORD made the heavens.” The parallel is Psalm 96:5.

Arminian readers note that the contrast between idols and the Creator calls the nations to turn from false gods, and they see the psalm inviting all peoples to recognize the true God who made the heavens.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the absolute difference between the Creator and the idols, and they link the verse with 14:12, where the Philistine gods were burned, as a reminder that the gods of the nations are powerless.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about the uniqueness of the LORD as Creator.

verses.text: Honor and majesty are before him. Strength and gladness are in his place.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Honor and majesty are before him. Strength and gladness are in his place.” The parallel in Psalm 96:6 reads “Strength and beauty are in his sanctuary”, and the difference is noted here rather than harmonized.

Arminian readers note that gladness fits the joyful setting of the ark’s arrival.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Chronicles speaks of his place, perhaps fitting a time before the temple was built, though the reason for the difference is not stated and should not be pressed.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about the majesty and joy of God’s presence, and they keep the two wordings side by side.

verses.text: Ascribe to the LORD, you families of the peoples, ascribe to the LORD glory and strength!
verses.arminianNotes:
“Ascribe to the LORD, you families of the peoples, ascribe to the LORD glory and strength!” The parallel in Psalm 96:7 reads “you families of nations”.

Arminian readers see the families of the peoples invited to join Israel in giving God glory, and they hear in this a genuine summons to all nations.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that ascribing glory means acknowledging what already belongs to God rather than adding to him, and they see the nations called to recognize the LORD’s rightful honor.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about worldwide worship, and they record the slight difference in wording between the two settings.

verses.text: Ascribe to the LORD the glory due to his name. Bring an offering, and come before him. Worship the LORD in holy array.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Ascribe to the LORD the glory due to his name. Bring an offering, and come before him. Worship the LORD in holy array.” The parallel in Psalm 96:8 reads “come into his courts”.

Arminian readers see worshipers invited to come before God with offerings and reverence.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the glory due to his name is rendered in worship marked by holiness, and they see the call to holy array as fitting after Chronicles’ emphasis on the consecration of priests and Levites (15:12–14).

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about reverent and joyful worship and record the difference in wording without harmonizing it.

verses.text: Tremble before him, all the earth. The world also is established that it can’t be moved.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Tremble before him, all the earth. The world also is established that it can’t be moved.” These lines correspond to Psalm 96:9–10.

Arminian readers note that trembling before God is the right response of creatures to their Maker, and they see the stability of the world as a sign of his faithful care for all he has made.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the establishment of the world reflects God’s sovereign rule, which holds creation firm, and they observe that Chronicles’ version does not include Psalm 96:10’s line “He will judge the peoples with equity”.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about awe before God and confidence in his rule.

verses.text: Let the heavens be glad, and let the earth rejoice! Let them say among the nations, “The LORD reigns!”
verses.arminianNotes:
The heavens are called to be glad and the earth to rejoice, and the nations are to hear the cry “The LORD reigns!” These lines correspond to Psalm 96:10–11, in a different order.

Arminian readers hear creation and the nations invited to rejoice in God’s reign.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the proclamation that the LORD reigns is the center of the psalm, and they see the whole created order summoned to celebrate his kingship, which the ark’s arrival in Jerusalem symbolizes in Israel’s worship.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about joy in God’s reign and record the different order of lines without harmonizing it.

verses.text: Let the sea roar, and its fullness! Let the field exult, and all that is in it!
verses.arminianNotes:
“Let the sea roar, and its fullness! Let the field exult, and all that is in it!” These lines correspond to Psalm 96:11–12.

Arminian readers see the whole creation joining in praise, and they note that the psalm invites the worshiper to see God’s goodness reflected in sea and field alike, so that all of creation becomes a choir of praise.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that creation’s praise is a poetic way of declaring that all things belong to God and exist for his glory, and they see the verse as part of the psalm’s wide horizon beyond Israel.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about the praise of all creation and treat its imagery as poetry, not as a point of doctrinal division.

verses.text: Then the trees of the forest will sing for joy before the LORD, for he comes to judge the earth.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Then the trees of the forest will sing for joy before the LORD, for he comes to judge the earth.” The parallel is Psalm 96:12–13, which reads woods and continues with “He will judge the world with righteousness, the peoples with his truth”.

Arminian readers hear God’s coming judgment as good news that creation welcomes.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the coming of the LORD to judge is presented as cause for joy, since his judgment sets the world right, and they read the verse as shared ground without a contrast over judgment.

Both traditions note that Chronicles’ version ends the Psalm 96 section at this point and record the difference without harmonizing it.

verses.text: Oh give thanks to the LORD, for he is good, for his loving kindness endures forever.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Oh give thanks to the LORD, for he is good, for his loving kindness endures forever.” This line matches the opening call of Psalm 106:1, and the refrain recurs in 16:41.

Arminian readers see the goodness and steadfast love of God as the deepest reason for thanksgiving, and they note that this refrain invites every generation to trust God’s character.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that God’s loving kindness is described as enduring forever, which they see as an assurance that his covenant love does not fail even when his people do, as the history recounted in the psalms makes plain.

Both traditions read the refrain as shared ground about the goodness and faithful love of God.

verses.text: Say, “Save us, God of our salvation! Gather us together and deliver us from the nations, to give thanks to your holy name, to triumph in your praise.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The people are told to say, “Save us, God of our salvation! Gather us together and deliver us from the nations, to give thanks to your holy name, to triumph in your praise.” The parallel in Psalm 106:47 reads “Save us, LORD, our God, gather us from among the nations”.

Arminian readers hear an earnest plea for rescue and restoration.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Chronicles itself looks back on Judah’s exile (9:1), and many readers hear this plea with the Chronicler’s later audience in mind, though the text does not say so directly.

Both traditions read the prayer as shared ground: God’s people ask him to save and gather them so that they may give thanks, and they record the differences in wording.

verses.text: Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, from everlasting even to everlasting. All the people said, “Amen,” and praised the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, from everlasting even to everlasting.” And all the people said, “Amen,” and praised the LORD. The parallel in Psalm 106:48 reads “Let all the people say”, while Chronicles reports that they did.

Arminian readers see the people’s response as a willing and heartfelt agreement with the praise offered.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the blessing of God from everlasting to everlasting places Israel’s worship within God’s eternal being, and they see the people’s Amen as the fitting close of the psalm.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about the whole community joining in praise, and they record the difference between the two settings without harmonizing it.
